learning_objective: 🎯 Crunch the numbers! Learn how to calculate cash flows, break-even points, and manage working capital to keep the business profitable!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: The measure of what you are selling. It could be a single physical item (a shirt), a unit of time (an hour of consulting), or a weight (1 kg of apples). It is the base unit for calculating revenue and costs.
The point where Total Revenue equals Total Costs. At the Break-Even Point (BEP), the business is making exactly zero profit and zero loss. Every unit sold *after* this point is pure profit.
A statement showing the expected cash inflows (money coming in) and cash outflows (money going out) over a specific period. Important rule: Profit does NOT equal Cash!
Managing the short-term assets and liabilities to ensure the business has enough liquid cash to pay for its day-to-day operations like rent, wages, and raw materials.
A profitability metric that evaluates the efficiency of an investment. Calculated as: (Net Profit / Total Investment) × 100. It tells you how much money you made relative to what you put in.

fun_activity.title: 🍋 Lemonade Stand Math
fun_activity.instructions: You start a lemonade stand. Your fixed costs (table, sign) are ₹100. It costs you ₹5 to make one cup (variable cost). You sell each cup for ₹15. How many cups do you need to sell to Break-Even? (Hint: Profit per cup is ₹10. ₹100 / 10 = ?)

exam_tips: 📌 The Break-Even Point formula is crucial: BEP = Total Fixed Costs / (Selling Price per unit - Variable Cost per unit).
📌 Remember the difference: Fixed costs stay the same regardless of production (e.g., rent), while variable costs change with production (e.g., raw materials).
📌 Always state that 'Gross Working Capital' = Total Current Assets, while 'Net Working Capital' = Current Assets - Current Liabilities.
quick_recap: ⭐ The difference between Selling Price and Variable Cost per unit is called 'Contribution'.
⭐ Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) helps a business determine the ideal order size to minimize inventory holding and ordering costs.
⭐ A business can be profitable on paper but still fail if it runs out of cash flow to pay its immediate bills.
